messages.subject: looping through a list and making plots in R?
parts:
I was wondering if I could perhaps do some kind of loop that will loop through 100 different locations and give me graphs of how many people visit a location and for that location give me the number of males and females that visit that location.

Suppose that:
-this data is stored in a csv files and i read it into R in a variable called data
- data$gender has male and female data so that when i do table(data$gender) i get the total overall number of females and males that visit each location
- data$location has these individual locations

gender_location <- by(data$gender,data$location,summary)

gives me the information i need like so:

data$location: 100
Female   Male 
     31    146 


how can i make it give me pie charts or bar graphs for each location via a loop? 

Your help is very much appreciated in advance!

messages.author: f4249b01b99d0091
messages.subject: Re: looping through a list and making plots in R?
parts:
This is somewhat unclear, but I assume that since you're posting this
to the ggplot list, you want help with the graphing (not the loop). A
minimal example would be:

library(ggplot2)
df <- data.frame(gender=c("M","F","F"))
p <- ggplot(df,aes(gender))+geom_bar()
print(p)

For a better answer, please provide a reproducible example...

HTH
Ben

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: looping through a list and making plots in R?
parts:
Hi:

I think this problem is a bit simpler than you're making it...

On Tue, Mar 4, 2014 at 10:19 AM, Loren V <lm.vela...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I was wondering if I could perhaps do some kind of loop that will loop
> through 100 different locations and give me graphs of how many people visit
> a location and for that location give me the number of males and females
> that visit that location.
>
> Suppose that:
> -this data is stored in a csv files and i read it into R in a variable
> called data
> - data$gender has male and female data so that when i do table(data$gender)
> i get the total overall number of females and males that visit each location
> - data$location has these individual locations

>
> gender_location <- by(data$gender,data$location,summary)

The problem with by() is that it returns a list, and you can't input a
list directly into ggplot2 - it has to be converted to a data frame
first.

The plyr package, also authored by Hadley Wickham, is a very good one
for basic data summarization. In this case, you could use the count()
function in that package to get the counts by location and gender
(which would return a data frame), but I would take it a bit further.
Rather than trying to plot bars and pies at each location, plot points
of the percentage of one gender instead. If the total number of
visitors is meaningful, then you could use something like color to
indicate percentage and point size to visualize the number of
visitors. They can be done together in ggplot2.

Inferring from your message, it appears that something like

library(plyr)
loccts <- count(data, c("location", "gender"))

would produce the frequencies and then

loccts <- ddply(loccts, .(location), mutate, N = sum(gender), prop = gender/N)

would add the sample size and proportions of males and females in each
location. You could then subset one of the genders and use that data
frame as input to a graphics package such as ggplot2. I don't know how
you planned on plotting your data, but you can use maps in ggplot2
with a bit of care, and it is possible to plot points at different
locations of a map (e.g., lat-long coordinates) either inside ggplot2
or with the ggmaps package.

If you insist on bars/pies per location, the ggsubplot package might
be helpful.

Dennis

> 31 146
>
>
> how can i make it give me pie charts or bar graphs for each location via a
> loop?
>
> Your help is very much appreciated in advance!

messages.author: f4249b01b99d0091
messages.subject: Re: looping through a list and making plots in R?
parts:
If you have only two or a few groups, many of us would use faceting, e.g.
print(ggplot(g,aes(gender))+geom_bar()+facet_grid(group~.))

For a lot of groups, as Dennis said plyr is a powerful option. A
simple loop-based alternative to plot gender ratios would look like
this:
for( i in unique(g$group)) {
df <- subset(g,group==i)
p <- ggplot(df, aes(gender) ) + geom_bar() + ggtitle(i)
print(p)
ggsave(paste0(i,".pdf")) # if you want to save plots
}

Ben

>> >>
>> >> Hi:
>> >>
>> >> I think this problem is a bit simpler than you're making it...
>> >>
>> >> On Tue, Mar 4, 2014 at 10:19 AM, Loren V <lm.vela...@gmail.com>
>> >> wrote:
>> >> > I was wondering if I could perhaps do some kind of loop that will
>> >> > loop
>> >> > through 100 different locations and give me graphs of how many people
>> >> > visit
>> >> > a location and for that location give me the number of males and
>> >> > females
>> >> > that visit that location.
>> >> >
>> >> > Suppose that:
>> >> > -this data is stored in a csv files and i read it into R in a
>> >> > variable
>> >> > called data
>> >> > - data$gender has male and female data so that when i do
>> >> > table(data$gender)
>> >> > i get the total overall number of females and males that visit each
>> >> > location
>> >> > - data$location has these individual locations
>> >>
>> >> >
>> >> > gender_location <- by(data$gender,data$location,summary)
>> >>
>> >> The problem with by() is that it returns a list, and you can't input a
>> >> list directly into ggplot2 - it has to be converted to a data frame
>> >> first.
>> >>
>> >> The plyr package, also authored by Hadley Wickham, is a very good one
>> >> for basic data summarization. In this case, you could use the count()
>> >> function in that package to get the counts by location and gender
>> >> (which would return a data frame), but I would take it a bit further.
>> >> Rather than trying to plot bars and pies at each location, plot points
>> >> of the percentage of one gender instead. If the total number of
>> >> visitors is meaningful, then you could use something like color to
>> >> indicate percentage and point size to visualize the number of
>> >> visitors. They can be done together in ggplot2.
>> >>
>> >> Inferring from your message, it appears that something like
>> >>
>> >> library(plyr)
>> >> loccts <- count(data, c("location", "gender"))
>> >>
>> >> would produce the frequencies and then
>> >>
>> >> loccts <- ddply(loccts, .(location), mutate, N = sum(gender), prop =
>> >> gender/N)
>> >>
>> >> would add the sample size and proportions of males and females in each
>> >> location. You could then subset one of the genders and use that data
>> >> frame as input to a graphics package such as ggplot2. I don't know how
>> >> you planned on plotting your data, but you can use maps in ggplot2
>> >> with a bit of care, and it is possible to plot points at different
>> >> locations of a map (e.g., lat-long coordinates) either inside ggplot2
>> >> or with the ggmaps package.
>> >>
>> >> If you insist on bars/pies per location, the ggsubplot package might
>> >> be helpful.
>> >>
>> >> Dennis
>> >>
>> >> >
>> >> > gives me the information i need like so:
>> >> >
>> >> > data$location: 100
>> >> > Female Male
>> >> > 31 146
>> >> >
>> >> >
>> >> > how can i make it give me pie charts or bar graphs for each location
>> >> > via
>> >> > a
>> >> > loop?
